{"say":"I marked the nine existing Driestromen places (gate, market, inn, Schorren, Tolwaard, ferry house, landing, cooperage and Wilgenwaard) as merges, so they keep their names and area instead of replacing the whole entry.","questions":[],"changes":[{"kind":"location","id":"loc_driestromen_gate","yaml":"id: loc_driestromen_gate
summary: "The walled gate where the long road from the Holleveen comes into the Driestromen."
sound:
  kind: crowd
  level: 0.5
  night: wind
description:
  day: "Walls of tarred brick stand higher than any in the Holleveen, and a wooden lantern for [Saint Brand] hangs in the arch. Carts wait in line to be let in, and the gatekeepers call to each other in quick, flat voices. The air smells of tar, smoke and river mud. The market opens just inside, and the long road north runs back along the dyke."
  night: "The great doors are barred for the night, but a wicket door with an iron grille still opens for a knock and a coin. Above the arch the lantern of [Saint Brand] burns low, yellow on wet brick. You hear the rivers moving somewhere beyond the walls. The market lies just inside."
details:
  - words: [lantern, wooden lantern]
    look: "A lantern of oak and horn, black with years of smoke, the saint's flame painted on each pane. The gatekeepers light it at dusk."
    take: "It hangs from a hook twice your height, and the gatekeepers would not let you near it."
  - words: [walls, wall, brick, tarred brick]
    look: "Brick upon brick, tarred black against the damp, with weed growing in the joints near the ground where the floods reach."
    verbs:
      climb: "The tar is slick and the joints too shallow. You get no higher than your own head."
  - words: [carts, cart]
    look: "Carts of salt, peat and barrel staves, their drivers leaning on the wheels and cursing the wait."
    take: "The nearest carter raps your knuckles with the butt of his whip."
  - words: [gatekeepers, gatekeeper]
    look: "Two men in leather jerkins with the Count's badge sewn on, one counting carts, the other counting coins."
  - words: [wicket door, wicket, door]
    look: "A small door cut into the great one, just wide enough for a person and a bundle."
    verbs:
      knock: "You knock. A face comes to the grille, looks you over, and a bolt slides back."
      open: "It is bolted from inside. You will have to knock."
  - words: [grille, iron grille]
    look: "A square of crossed iron bars at face height, rusted where hands have held it."
    take: "It is riveted into the oak."
  - words: [dyke, road, dyke road]
    look: "The road runs north along the crown of the dyke, back towards the Holleveen, two days away on foot."
    take: "You pick up a clod of dyke clay. It is only mud; you let it fall."

summary: "The brick market square where the roads of the Driestromen meet, with its hated toll board."
sound:
  kind: crowd
  level: 0.7
  night: quiet
description:
  day: "Stalls of salt, cloth and eel-pots crowd the worn brick square, and traders shout their prices over each other. Pitch and hot fat drift from the cookshops. On a post in the middle a toll board lists what [the Count] takes on every barge, and someone has scratched the numbers out. The Carters' Inn leans at the corner, and the gate is back out."
  night: "The stalls are folded and roped under tarred canvas, and the square is empty but for cats and a watchman's lamp. The smell of fish and pitch has sunk into the brick. The toll board of [the Count] still stands on its post, pale in the lamplight. Light and noise spill from the Carters' Inn at the corner."

details:
  - words: [stalls, stall]
    look: "Trestles under striped awnings, heaped with grey sea salt, bolts of Flemmark cloth, and wicker eel-pots stacked like beehives."
    take: "The stallholder's hand is on your wrist before your fingers close. You let go."
  - words: [eel-pots, eel pots, pots]
    look: "Long wicker traps, narrow at one end, woven in the Wilgenwaard."
    take: "Ask the stallholder the price first."
  - words: [cookshops, cookshop]
    look: "Open hatches in the house fronts, where fat spits in iron pans and eels turn on skewers."
    verbs:
      smell: "Hot fat, burnt eel skin and onions. Your stomach answers."
  - words: [post]
    look: "A thick oak post driven into the brick, scarred with nails where old notices hung."
    take: "It is set deep in the ground."
  - words: [toll board, board, numbers]
    look: "A painted board with the Count's arms at the top and a column of tolls beneath, per cask, per last of grain, per barge."
    take: "It is nailed to the post with nails as long as your finger."
    verbs:
      read: "Where the numbers were, someone has scratched deep grooves with a knife. Underneath, in small letters, it still says 'bound for Flemmark'."
  - words: [canvas, tarred canvas]
    look: "Stiff black canvas roped down over the folded stalls."
    take: "It is roped tight, and it is somebody's living."
  - words: [watchman's lamp, lamp, watchman]
    look: "A lamp on a pole, carried slowly round the square by a man in a hooded cloak."
  - words: [cats, cat]
    look: "Thin market cats, nosing the gaps between the bricks for fish scraps."
    take: "The cat slides out of your hands and away."

summary: "A low, loud inn where the carters of the Three Rivers drink and sleep."
sound:
  kind: hearth
  level: 0.6
description:
  day: "Beams hang so low you duck under them, and carters from half the land sit over their beer at long tables. It is warm and loud, and it smells of wet wool, onions and spilt ale. Over the hearth hangs an old ferry oar, black with smoke, carved with the names of drowned men. The market is back out."
  night: "The tables are full and the fire is built high, and every voice has to shout to be heard. Wet wool steams on the benches nearest the hearth. The carved ferry oar glints in the firelight above the heads of the drinkers. The door back out to the market lets in a breath of cold river air."
details:
  - words: [ferry oar, oar]
    look: "A long ash oar, worn smooth at the grip, its blade covered in cut names and little crosses."
    take: "It hangs on iron pegs over the fire, and the carters would not like you touching it."
    verbs:
      read: "Names and years, the oldest too worn to make out. The newest are cut deep and clean."
  - words: [long tables, tables, table]
    look: "Planks on trestles, ringed with beer and cut with carters' marks."
  - words: [beer, ale]
    look: "Brown beer in wooden cans. The innkeeper sells it."
    take: "That can belongs to a carter with fists like mallets."
  - words: [hearth, fire]
    look: "A wide brick hearth burning peat and driftwood, with a kettle on a hook."
  - words: [carters, carter]
    look: "Big men and a few big women in muddy boots, talking of roads, tolls and the price of a night's grazing."

summary: "Salt marsh and tidal mud at the seaward edge, where the eel-folk live on stilts."
sound:
  kind: birds
  level: 0.5
  night: wind
description:
  day: "Beyond the last dyke the land gives up and becomes salt marsh, grey-green samphire and creeks of shining mud. The wind off the Grey Sea tastes of salt, and gulls wheel crying overhead. Eel-folk huts stand on stilts along a plank walk, nets hung between them to dry. Out on the flats to the east, they say, you can hear [the drowned bells of Saeftinge]."
  night: "The marsh is black, and the creeks catch what little light the sky has. The tide whispers as it fills them. A lantern swings on the last stilt hut along the plank walk. The eel-folk do not go out on the mud at night; the market is back southwest."
exits:
  southwest:
    to: loc_driestromen_market
    minutes: 5
  east:
    to: loc_driestromen_bell_flats
    minutes: 15
details:
  - words: [samphire, marsh, salt marsh]
    look: "Fleshy green shoots growing thick on the mud, salty to taste."
    take: "You pull a handful. It is sour and salt; the eel-folk pickle it."
  - words: [creeks, creek, mud]
    look: "Winding channels in the grey mud, full or empty with the tide."
  - words: [huts, hut, stilt hut, stilts]
    look: "Shacks of tarred planks on legs of alder, ladders drawn up at the doors."
    verbs:
      climb: "The ladders are drawn up. Whoever lives here does not want visitors unasked."
  - words: [plank walk, walk, planks]
    look: "Planks laid end to end on posts over the mud, slick and soft with salt."
    take: "Pull up a plank and someone ends up in the mud. Perhaps you."
  - words: [nets, net]
    look: "Brown nets hung on poles, stiff with salt, a few holes being mended."
    take: "They are not yours, and the eel-folk count them."
  - words: [gulls, gull]
    look: "Grey-backed gulls, loud and quarrelsome."
  - words: [lantern]
    look: "A horn lantern swinging on a hook by a hut door."
    take: "It hangs from the hut, out of reach."

summary: "The island on the third river where barges wait for the Count's toll and his chain bars the way to Flemmark."
sound:
  kind: water
  level: 0.5
description:
  day: "A narrow plank bridge carries you onto the island, where barges lie moored three deep waiting for the toll. Tar and river water smell strong here, and the great chain groans as the current leans on it. The toll house of [the Count] stands at the point, its shutters painted in his colours. The market is back east over the bridge."
  night: "Lamps burn in the toll house windows, and a watchman walks the moored barges with a pike. The chain lies across the black water and groans when the current leans. On a moonless night, the boatmen say, a skiff can slip under it where it sags. The bridge back to the market is east."
exits:
  east:
    to: loc_driestromen_market
    minutes: 5
  in:
    to: loc_driestromen_toll_house
    minutes: 1
details:
  - words: [bridge, plank bridge]
    look: "Planks on tarred piles, just wide enough for a handcart, bouncing underfoot."
    take: "The planks are pegged down hard."
  - words: [barges, barge]
    look: "Broad river barges laden with grain, casks and peat, their skippers sitting on the hatches, waiting and grumbling."
    verbs:
      board: "A skipper looks up sharply. You step back onto the bank."
  - words: [chain, great chain]
    look: "Links as thick as your wrist, stretched from a winch on the island to a post on the far bank, sagging into the brown water in the middle."
    take: "It weighs more than a horse."
  - words: [shutters]
    look: "Shutters painted red and gold, the paint peeling where boatmen have spat on it."
  - words: [watchman, pike]
    look: "A heavy man with a pike over his shoulder and a lantern at his belt."
  - words: [far bank, flemmark bank, flemmark]
    look: "A low grey line across the water, with willows and a tower. That is Flemmark."

summary: "The ferry house at the end of the Veerdijk, on the first river."
sound:
  kind: hearth
  level: 0.4
  night: water
description:
  day: "Low walls of tarred brick lean against the dyke, and the door stands open to the river wind. Inside you smell wet rope, peat smoke and eel fat spitting on the hearth. A slate by the fire shows the fares, and under it a chalked horse is struck through, for [the Grey Rider's fare]. A plank path runs out the back door down to the landing."
  night: "The hearth is banked to a red glow, and the ferryman's boots stand drying beside it. Rope and peat smoke hang in the warm air. The fare slate shows its struck-out horse in the firelight, and after the lamps are lit nobody crosses while a grey horse waits. The back door to the landing is shut on the dark."
details:
  - words: [slate, fares, fare slate]
    look: "A slate the size of a shutter, the fares in stuivers and duiten chalked over many times."
    take: "It is nailed by the fire, and the ferryman lives by it."
    verbs:
      read: "A person, two duiten. A person with a pack, three. A cart and horse, two stuivers. Nothing after the lamps are lit."
  - words: [horse, chalked horse]
    look: "A small horse drawn in chalk under the fares, with a hard line struck through it."
    take: "You could rub it out. The ferryman would only chalk it again."
  - words: [plank path, path, back door]
    look: "Planks laid on the dyke slope down to the water, slick with river damp."
  - words: [hearth, fire]
    look: "A low hearth of yellow brick, where eel fat spits in a pan."
  - words: [rope]
    look: "Coils of spare ferry rope, wet and heavy, hanging by the door."
    take: "It is the ferryman's spare rope. He would miss it."

summary: "The landing on the first river, with a bell to call the ferry."
sound:
  kind: water
  level: 0.6
description:
  day: "The dyke road gives out here in trodden mud and a flat boat tied to a rope strung across the brown water. A bell hangs from a post, its cord green with damp; one clang brings the ferryman. You hear the rope creak on its pulleys and the tide sucking at the reeds. The ferry house is back up the path to the south."
  night: "The flat boat lies still at its rope, and the river is a wide dark sound. The bell on its post hangs silent; after the lamps are lit it brings nobody. Reeds hiss in the wind along the bank. The lit window of the ferry house is back up the path."
details:
  - words: [flat boat, boat, ferry]
    look: "A broad flat-bottomed boat of tarred planks, big enough for a cart and horse, with a rail along each side."
    verbs:
      board: "You step onto the boards. It rocks and settles. Without the ferryman it goes nowhere."
  - words: [rope, pulleys]
    look: "A thick hemp rope strung across the river from post to post, running through iron pulleys on the boat."
    take: "It is strung taut across the whole river."
  - words: [bell]
    look: "A bronze bell the size of a pail, dull green, with a cord hanging from its clapper."
    take: "It is bolted to the post."
    verbs:
      ring: "One clang rolls out over the water. On the far bank someone stirs."
  - words: [post, cord]
    look: "A weathered post with the bell on an iron arm, its cord green with damp."
  - words: [willow islands, islands]
    look: "Across the river, low grey islands of willow, each with a small dyke round it."
  - words: [reeds]
    look: "Tall reeds along the bank, sucking and whispering with the tide."
    take: "You snap off a reed. It is hollow and smells of river."

summary: "A cooper's yard on the dyke, making casks for eels and herring."
sound:
  kind: workshop
  level: 0.6
  night: quiet
description:
  day: "Barrel staves lie stacked against a shed on the dyke's inner slope, bleaching in the wind. You hear the knock of a mallet on hoops long before you reach the door. Half-built casks for eels and herring crowd the yard, smelling of fresh oak. A cart track bends from here back toward the market."
  night: "The yard is dark and the mallet is silent. Half-built casks stand about like crouching figures, and the stacked staves smell of oak and dew. The shed door is shut and padlocked. The cart track runs back toward the market."
details:
  - words: [staves, barrel staves]
    look: "Split oak staves, curved and tapered, stacked in crossed piles to season."
    take: "You lift one. It is heavy, and it is the cooper's."
  - words: [shed]
    look: "A tarred plank shed with a wide door, tools hung on pegs inside."
  - words: [mallet]
    look: "A heavy wooden mallet, its head bound in iron."
    take: "The cooper keeps it close."
  - words: [hoops, hoop]
    look: "Iron hoops and split willow hoops, hung on the shed wall by size."
  - words: [casks, cask]
    look: "Squat casks for salted eels, taller ones for herring, some still open at the top."
    take: "They are half made, and too big to carry off."

summary: "Willow islands between the first and second rivers, with osier beds and houses on mounds."
sound:
  kind: reeds
  level: 0.5
  night: water
description:
  day: "Willow islands crowd between the first and second rivers, each ringed by its own knee-high dyke, and the houses stand on mounds with their feet dry. Osier beds rustle on every side, cut back to red stumps. You smell eel smoke from a smokehouse where the catch hangs in rows. Plank bridges run on south to the weirs; the market is back north."
  night: "The willows are black shapes over black water, and the plank bridges creak underfoot. Lamps glow in the windows of the houses up on their mounds. Somewhere a dog barks, and the rivers answer with their long murmur. The market is back north."

details:
  - words: [dyke, dykes, knee-high dyke]
    look: "A little dyke of turf and clay round each island, no higher than your knee, patched with fresh sods."
    take: "You could kick a sod loose, and someone's floor would be wet by spring."
  - words: [mounds, mound, houses]
    look: "Brick houses on raised mounds of earth, their doors a man's height above the paths."
  - words: [osier beds, osiers, stumps]
    look: "Rows of cut willow, the stumps red where the rods were taken for baskets and eel-pots."
    take: "You pull a rod. It bends supple as a whip. Someone owns this bed."
  - words: [smokehouse, eels, catch]
    look: "A squat brick smokehouse with a louvred roof, eels hanging inside in golden rows."
    take: "The door is latched, and the smoker is near."
  - words: [plank bridges, bridges, bridge]
    look: "Planks on stakes from island to island, some with a rope for a rail."
  - words: [willows, willow]
    look: "Pollard willows with heads of new shoots, their trunks split and hollow."
